questions.stem: What is image classification in Computer Vision, and how does it differ from object detection and semantic segmentation?
options: Image classification predicts bounding boxes around individual objects and their locations within a photograph. Object detection chooses a single category for the complete image, while segmentation describes exclusively an photograph's original dimensions and color settings.

Image classification predicts a category for an entire image by recognizing visual patterns. Object detection also locates individual objects, while semantic segmentation assigns class labels to pixels, providing more detailed spatial information than classification alone.

Image classification assigns a separate class label to every pixel instead of predicting an overall image category. Object detection examines whole-image labels only, while segmentation identifies the particular camera or device that captured the scene.

Image classification determines whether an image is visually sharp or blurry without learning categories. Object detection estimates the resolution, while semantic segmentation compresses the original picture into smaller numerical tiles before the classifier processes it.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Image classification answers 'What category best describes this image?' A pet-photo classifier might output 'cat' for a picture. It does not automatically say where the cat is. Object detection predicts labels and locations, often as bounding boxes. Semantic segmentation labels pixels to show where different classes appear. For example, a road-scene classifier may identify 'street,' while segmentation can outline road, sidewalk, and vehicles. A single-label classifier chooses one category; multilabel classification can assign several.

questions.stem: How do image tensors, resizing, normalization, and data augmentation prepare images for training without leaking information into evaluation?
options: Convert images into tensors and change the validation labels whenever training performance drops. Normalize the test images, since training images should retain inconsistent sizes to help the network learn scale automatically.

Resize images into identical shapes, then apply random transformations to training and test data at every evaluation step. This guarantees stable test scores even when the model sees content across runs.

Convert images into tensors, then compute feature-normalization statistics using held-out evaluation examples because it prevents measurement bias. Shuffle near-duplicate images across splits so the network is evaluated on familiar visual scenes.

Resize images, create channel-first pixel tensors, and normalize with training statistics. Use label-preserving random augmentation during training, apply fixed transforms to validation and test sets, and separate images from related sources.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A CNN expects numeric image tensors, commonly shaped channels × height × width for one image in PyTorch. Resize images to a consistent input size and normalize pixel values appropriately. Random crops, flips, or color changes can increase training diversity if they preserve labels. Validation and test preprocessing should usually be deterministic. For example, if images from the same patient or camera session appear in both training and test sets, leakage can make accuracy look better than real-world performance.

questions.stem: How does a convolutional neural network turn image pixels into class predictions using filters, feature maps, pooling, logits, and softmax?
options: Convolutional filters learn spatial patterns and produce feature maps. Deeper layers combine these features, pooling summarizes spatial information, and a classification head generates raw logits. Softmax converts logits to class probabilities for single-label inference.

Convolutional filters directly store the final category for each training image, while feature maps simply preserve file names. Pooling restores original pixel resolution, and softmax updates network weights before any loss or optimizer calculation.

Convolutional filters compare each pixel against a permanently fixed list of class names without learning spatial patterns. Pooling selects one random pixel, logits are ground-truth labels, and softmax changes the dataset labels during training.

Convolutional filters calculate image compression ratios, and feature maps represent only file sizes rather than learned patterns. Pooling adds missing pixels, logits are optimizer gradients, and softmax automatically guarantees reliable predictions on unfamiliar images.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A CNN uses learned convolutional filters to detect visual patterns. Early filters may respond to edges, while deeper features can represent parts or textures. Pooling or global average pooling summarizes spatial information. A final linear layer produces logits, which are raw class scores. Softmax can turn logits into a probability distribution for single-label prediction. For PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss, pass raw logits rather than applying softmax first. Inference typically selects the class with the highest score.

questions.stem: How would you implement a simple image classifier in PyTorch, compute cross-entropy loss, update weights, and generate predicted class labels?
options: Build a convolutional network and convert image tensors into incorrect integer class IDs before the actual forward pass. Compute CrossEntropyLoss from filenames instead of logits, skip backpropagation, and use the largest input pixel as the prediction.

Build a convolutional network that returns probabilities by applying argmax before the loss calculation. Optimize those non-differentiable discrete class labels with CrossEntropyLoss, then completely skip subsequent weight updates because the model already selected the winning class.

Build a neural network with convolution, activation, pooling, and a classification head. Run image batches through it to produce raw logits, compute CrossEntropyLoss against integer class IDs, backpropagate, update the optimizer, and use argmax for predictions.

Build a convolutional network with pooling and a classification head, then compute CrossEntropyLoss only on predicted human-readable class names. Keep the optimizer fixed, update validation labels after every batch, and report training accuracy as final performance.
questions.explanation: Explanation: In PyTorch, a basic classifier can combine Conv2d, ReLU, pooling, and a linear output layer. For three classes, the model produces three logits per image. CrossEntropyLoss compares those raw logits with integer target IDs. Call backward to compute gradients and optimizer.step to update parameters. During inference, use eval mode and no_grad, then take argmax across class logits. The example below demonstrates one training step on random synthetic tensors; meaningful classification requires labeled photographs, multiple batches, and held-out evaluation.

questions.figure:
04 · VISUAL LESSON

Train a small CNN and predict

PyTorch · toy CNN training and prediction 16 lines
01 import torch
02 from torch import nn
03 net = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(3, 8, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
04                     nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(8, 3))
05 x = torch.randn(4, 3, 32, 32)
06 y = torch.tensor([0, 1, 2, 1])
07 opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
08 opt.zero_grad()
09 logits = net(x)
10 loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(logits, y)
11 loss.backward()
12 opt.step()
13 net.eval()
14 with torch.no_grad():
15     predicted = net(x).argmax(dim=1)
16 print("logits", tuple(logits.shape), "predicted", predicted.tolist())

CPU-friendly PyTorch example using random synthetic images and three classes. It verifies tensor shapes, loss, gradients and prediction mechanics, not model accuracy. Real training needs labeled data and held-out tests.

PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss consumes raw logits and class IDs; argmax chooses the predicted category.

questions.stem: How can transfer learning adapt a pretrained image classifier to new categories while controlling data leakage and uneven class frequencies?
options: Reuse a pretrained backbone and leave its original pretrained classifier unchanged even when the target categories differ. Split near-duplicate images across training, validation, and testing, then repeatedly increase batch size until minority classes become equally frequent automatically.

Reuse a pretrained visual backbone, replace its classification head with outputs for the new classes, and fine-tune appropriate layers. Keep related images in the same data split and address class imbalance with sampling, weighting, and per-class evaluation.

Permanently discard every pretrained visual feature layer and copy only the original pretrained final class scores into a arbitrary new model. Place photographs from one subject across every data split, then judge adaptation using training loss alone.

Reuse pretrained convolutional layers but completely freeze the newly replaced classification head before any further supervised training. Apply balancing only by deleting all minority examples, and report overall validation accuracy without inspecting which classes are being missed.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Transfer learning starts from a model that has learned useful image features. Replace its final classifier so the output count matches your task, then train the head or fine-tune selected backbone layers. For example, a plant-disease model may start with an ImageNet-pretrained backbone and learn five crop conditions. Split related photos by plant, location, or collection session to avoid leakage. When classes are uneven, consider class-weighted loss or sampling and report per-class recall and F1, not just overall accuracy.

questions.stem: Why can a classifier show high overall accuracy while missing important minority classes, and how should engineers evaluate such failures?
options: Overall accuracy always measures every class equally, so a strong value guarantees strong rare-class recall. Confusion matrices are only needed for object detection, while calibration and distribution shifts cannot affect image classification decisions.

Overall accuracy becomes unreliable only when every class has identical frequency in the training data. For imbalanced datasets, random test-set accuracy is always sufficient, and per-class statistical performance measures create unnecessary evaluation noise.

Overall accuracy reports the number of pixels labeled correctly rather than the fraction of classified images. It therefore cannot be compared with confusion matrices, and minority-class recall applies only to specialized segmentation models.

Overall accuracy can hide poor performance on rare classes when common examples dominate the dataset. Inspect the confusion matrix, per-class precision and recall, macro-F1, calibration, and robustness on representative held-out and shifted images.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine a test set containing 95 common examples and five rare examples. If a model correctly classifies 94 common images and only one rare image, while making five mistakes, accuracy is 95%, but rare-class recall is just 1/5 = 20%. The confusion matrix reveals this gap. Inspect per-class precision and recall, macro-F1, and score calibration. Test across lighting, cameras, backgrounds, and user populations; an excellent average score can hide critical failures.

questions.stem: How would you deploy an image classifier to a mobile or edge device while maintaining latency, reliability, privacy, and model quality?
options: Export a model to a supported runtime, verify identical preprocessing and class mappings, and benchmark real-device latency and memory. Evaluate quantization accuracy, monitor input drift and confidence, protect image privacy, and version deployments for rollback.

Deploy only the network weights without preserving the training preprocessing or class label order. Assume desktop accuracy automatically guarantees edge accuracy, ignore image privacy because predictions are numeric, and update deployed models without version tracking.

Apply quantization to reduce file size and assume it always improves accuracy, latency, and calibration on every available processor. Skip real-device performance measurements, and stop monitoring after the application successfully loads the model one time.

Convert images to whichever resolution the device camera provides without independently validating the model's expected input contract. Measure training accuracy as the acceptance test, and disable rollback because edge devices cannot support multiple versioned releases.
questions.explanation: Explanation: An edge image classifier must work within real device limits. Export in a supported format and keep resizing, normalization, and class-index mappings consistent with training. Benchmark latency, memory, and energy using realistic images. Quantization may save resources but can change predictions, so compare accuracy before and after conversion. For example, an offline defect-inspection camera should monitor lighting changes and false negatives. Protect stored images, track model versions, and provide a rollback path when performance worsens.
